description_full: Energy Transfer LP, together with its subsidiaries, provides energy-related services in the United States. It operates through Intrastate Transportation and Storage; Interstate Transportation and Storage; Midstream; Natural Gas Liquid (NGL) and Refined Products Transportation and Services; Crude Oil Transportation and Services; Investment in Sunoco LP; Investment in USA Compression Partners, LP (USAC); and All Other segments. The company owns and operates natural gas transportation pipelines and storage facilities; and approximately 12,200 miles of intrastate natural gas transportation pipelines and 20,090 miles of interstate natural gas pipelines. It also sells natural gas to electric utilities, independent power plants, local distribution and other marketing companies, and industrial end-users. In addition, the company owns and operates natural gas gathering pipelines, processing plants, and treating and conditioning facilities; and natural gas gathering, compression, treating, dehydration and processing, oil pipeline facilities. Further, it owns 5,700 miles of NGL pipelines; NGL fractionation and storage facilities; and other NGL storage assets and terminals. Additionally, the company provides crude oil transportation, terminalling, trucking, acquisition, and marketing activities; owns and operates approximately 18,000 miles of crude oil trunk and gathering pipelines; and sells and distributes motor fuels and other petroleum products under the Sunoco and EcoMaxx brands. It also offers natural gas compression; wholesale power trading; and carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide removal services, as well as management of coal and natural resources properties; sells standing timber; leases coal-related infrastructure facilities; and collects oil and gas royalties. The company was formerly known as Energy Transfer Equity, L.P. and changed its name to Energy Transfer LP in October 2018. Energy Transfer LP was founded in 1996 and is headquartered in Dallas, Texas.

financial_summary: Energy Transfer LP is a large-cap energy business with a $66.8B market cap on $85.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $3.8B in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.29× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 7.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 10% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.2) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Payout ratio of 89% leaves thin coverage if earnings wobble
Carries more leverage than most Energy peers — a smaller cushion for the inevitable bad year
The commodity cycle — revenue and free cash flow are ultimately hostage to a price the company does not set, and the long-run energy-transition arc adds a structural overhang.
ESG-driven capital flight and stranded asset risk — tightening climate policy and investor mandates raise the cost of capital and risk leaving reserves permanently in the ground.
Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.

sect: Its 11% operating margin trails the Energy median (16%) by 5pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.97x).
It accounts for 2.2% of sector revenue and 2.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-20.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 30% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 18% and a beta of 0.64, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.10 vs 5y 0.57), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $162.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 66% in the 2020 crash, 22% in the 2022 bear market and 60% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 7% below its DCF fair value of $20.77, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 36%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $11.35 to $34.33 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 63% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $24.74 on average, 28% above the price.
The price implies 3.8% annual cash-flow growth, 1pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.37).
It runs a 18% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.29x.
ROE of 13% is amplified by 4.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.6x net debt to EBITDA ($1.3B of cash against $68.3B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.6x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.22 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.6% over 3 years, 17.0% over 5 years and 7.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 54%).
At current returns, reinvesting 28% of profits supports about 2.6% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.95 and a backlog worth 39% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 7.4% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 21, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 10.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 33%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (5 purchases, net $55.3M bought).
It returns 7.1% a year to shareholders (7.1% in dividends).
The share count has grown 4.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 19 consecutive years.
people: With about 22,311 employees, each generates about $3.8M of revenue, 1.9x the Energy median, and revenue has grown 18.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $172K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.3M (1x revenue per employee).
